source.version: arXiv:2211.14228v6 (30 May 2023), manuscript dated May 31, 2023; full text including Appendices A-E.
source.title_on_document: GPT-3-driven pedagogical agents for training children’s curious question-asking skills

supplement.holds: Cue relatedness and divergence rating grids; criteria for accepting children’s questions; the question-quality scoring rubric; and supplementary analyses of curiosity-trait associations. No additional arm means or standard errors for the main training contrasts are supplied.

paper_design_summary: The paper first compares GPT-3-generated pedagogical cues with human-generated cues using researcher annotations (pp. 5-6, 17-18, 21-23). Its school field study recruited 75 children and assigned them by a method described as pseudo-randomized after baseline profiling to hand-crafted incentive cues, GPT-3 incentive cues, or GPT-3 open keyword cues; the allocation algorithm and final analyzed counts are not specified (p. 18, section 6.2.1). Children generated questions about reading texts with these cues, and researchers scored their divergence and question quality; an offline question-generation test was also given before and after training (pp. 16, 18-20, 24-27).

studies.label: Pedagogical cue evaluation: GPT-3 versus human-generated output

assignment.what_was_assigned: No people were allocated to AI assistance in this component; the comparison is between cues generated by human experts and cues generated by GPT-3.
assignment.quote: In a first step, we use GPT-3 to generate curiosity-eliciting cues and compare them to what human experts can produce when given the same task.
assignment.locator: p. 5, section 3, first step; pp. 17-18, section 6.1; pp. 21-23, section 8.1.

arms.name: Hand-crafted incentive cues
arms.description: Human-generated questioning words and answer-like semantic cues leading to specific divergent questions (pp. 7-8, section 4.1).

arms.name: GPT-3 incentive cues
arms.description: GPT-3-generated questioning words and answer-like semantic cues leading to specific divergent questions (p. 8, section 4.1).

arms.name: GPT-3 open cues
arms.description: GPT-3-generated keywords and questioning words allowing multiple possible questions (p. 8, section 4.1).

participants.who: This component analyzes a corpus of cues. Human control cues were chosen by researchers and teachers; the number of human cue producers is not stated. The researcher annotators are raters, not participants receiving AI assistance.
participants.quote: For the Group 1, these cues were chosen by researchers and teachers as they were judged to be leading to important questions for children to ask.
participants.locator: p. 8, section 4.1; pp. 17-18, section 6.1. No people or cue counts are explicitly reported for the cue comparison.

ai_tool.how_used: Prompted offline to generate linguistic and semantic cues about educational reading texts. Outputs were checked, translated into French using DeepL, and stored for later presentation to children (pp. 12-14, section 4.4).

task.description: Generate pedagogical cues that support divergent questions about reading texts; researchers evaluate cue relevance, linguistic properties, and divergence (pp. 17-18, section 6.1).

outcomes.name: Divergence level of incentive semantic cues relative to the source text
outcomes.question: none

contrasts.reported: Hand-crafted incentive cues versus GPT-3 incentive cues: no significant difference in divergence scores; t=0.9, p-value=0.37 and power=0.14. This comparison concerns the cues, not children’s questions.
contrasts.locator: p. 23, section 8.1.3 and Figure 9(b); p. 31, Appendix B, divergence-rating grid.

studies.label: School field intervention with reported pseudo-randomized allocation

assignment.what_was_assigned: Children were assigned to hand-crafted incentive, GPT-3 incentive, or GPT-3 open cues after collection of baseline profiles. The authors call the method pseudo-randomized but do not specify whether it used random draws or deterministic balancing; actual random assignment cannot be established.
assignment.quote: The groups were assigned with a pseudo-randomized method after collecting profile data regarding the age, digital device use frequency, curiosity related measures, reading fluency and the domain-knowledge scores (see 6 for more details of the measures).
assignment.locator: p. 18, section 6.2.1; p. 27, section 8.4.1, between-condition and within-person pre/post analysis.

arms.name: Hand-crafted incentive agent (Group 1)
arms.description: Questioning words plus human-generated answer cues leading toward predefined divergent questions; an active non-generative-AI aid (pp. 7-8, section 4.1). Assigned 24 children; final analyzed count not stated (p. 18, section 6.2.1).

arms.name: GPT-3 incentive agent (Group 2)
arms.description: Questioning words plus GPT-3-generated answer cues leading toward predefined divergent questions (p. 8, section 4.1). Assigned 26 children; final analyzed count not stated (p. 18, section 6.2.1).

arms.name: GPT-3 open agent (Group 3)
arms.description: GPT-3-generated keyword cues with questioning-word support, allowing several possible divergent questions (p. 8, section 4.1). Assigned 25 children; final analyzed count not stated (p. 18, section 6.2.1).

participants.exclusions: Participant exclusions and final analyzed counts are not explicitly reported. The question acceptance rules exclude invalid, irrelevant, or repeated outputs; they do not establish participant exclusions (pp. 18-19, section 6.2.2; pp. 31-32, Appendix C).
participants.who: 75 fourth-grade children aged 9 to 10.5 years were recruited from three classes in two French primary schools. The assigned group sizes were 24 for the hand-crafted incentive agent, 26 for the GPT-3 incentive agent, and 25 for the GPT-3 open agent. These are recruited/assigned counts; final analyzed counts are not explicitly stated (p. 18, section 6.2.1).
participants.quote: We recruited 75 4th grade students from three classes in two French primary schools.
participants.locator: p. 18, section 6.2.1: 75 recruited children and assigned group sizes 24, 26, 25; pp. 24-25, sections 8.2.1-8.2.2, and p. 27, section 8.4.1, report results without explicit final analyzed counts.

ai_tool.name_model: Kids Ask conversational agents using offline GPT-3 text-davinci-002 cues
ai_tool.how_used: Children received previously generated linguistic and semantic cues through the agent while composing their questions. GPT-3 outputs were checked, translated into French with DeepL, and stored in a database; children did not chat directly with GPT-3. The control agent used human-generated cues (pp. 7-8, 13-14, sections 4.1 and 4.4).

task.description: Children worked individually on tablets, generating six questions for each of three reading texts (18 requested questions) using their assigned cues. Offline pre/post tests asked them to generate as many questions as possible about a short text without the agent (p. 16, section 5; p. 20, section 6.4.1).
task.duration: Three sessions within the same week. Section 5 describes each as 1h (p. 14), whereas Figure 4 labels the pre-training and post-training sessions 1h and the QA-training session 1h15 (p. 15); the training-session duration is internally inconsistent. Each offline question-generation test lasted 2 minutes (p. 20, section 6.4.1).

outcomes.name: Percentage of accepted questions classified as divergent during training
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: For each participant, the percentage of accepted, nonduplicate training questions classified as divergent because the answer is not explicitly stated in the text. Relevant questions were accepted even if they did not use the agent’s cues (pp. 18-19, section 6.2.2; pp. 31-32, Appendix C). The same two researcher coders evaluated the questions; reported inter-rater reliability was 87.6% (pp. 17-19, sections 6.1-6.2.2). The three-group omnibus comparison was F(2,72)=4.11, p-value=0.02 (p. 24, section 8.2.1); pairwise contrasts are recorded separately.

contrasts.reported: GPT-3 open agent versus hand-crafted incentive agent: the open-agent group had a higher percentage of divergent questions; t=-3.17, p-value=0.003 and power=0.82. The sign of t is reproduced as printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 24, section 8.2.1 and Figure 10(a); pp. 18-19, section 6.2.2, outcome definition; pp. 31-32, Appendix C, acceptance criteria.

contrasts.reported: No significant difference between hand-crafted and GPT-3 incentive agents in the percentage of divergent questions: t=0.88, p-value=0.38 and power=0.14. The t statistic is reproduced in the source’s comparison order.
contrasts.locator: p. 24, section 8.2.1 and Figure 10(a); pp. 7-8, section 4.1, condition definitions.

contrasts.reported: The GPT-3 open-agent group had a higher percentage of divergent questions than the GPT-3 incentive-agent group: t=-1.88, p=0.04 and power=0.45. The sign of t is reproduced as printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 24, section 8.2.1 and Figure 10(a); p. 8, section 4.1, condition definitions.

outcomes.name: Offline divergent question-asking fluency before and after training
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of divergent questions produced without the agent in an offline task asking children to write as many questions as possible about a short text within 2 minutes, using the same annotation method as the training questions (p. 20, section 6.4.1). The post-test in Session 3 is the after_ai outcome; the Session 1 pre-test is its baseline and is not itself an after_ai outcome (pp. 14-16, section 5 and Figure 4; p. 27, section 8.4.1).
outcomes.delay: Exact delay in days not stated; the post-test was in a separate post-intervention session within the same week (pp. 14-16, section 5 and Figure 4).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Omnibus condition-by-time comparison across Hand-crafted incentive agent (Group 1); GPT-3 incentive agent (Group 2); GPT-3 open agent (Group 3)
contrasts.control_arm: No single control arm: pre/post changes compared across all three conditions
contrasts.reported: The three conditions did not differ significantly in pre/post change: condition:time F(2,72)=2.23, p=0.11. The paper also reports time F(2,72)=46.95, p-value<0.001 and condition F(2,72)=3.9, p-value=0.002. Direction refers to the condition-by-time interaction. These are omnibus repeated-measures results, not pairwise AI-versus-control estimates; statistics and degrees of freedom are reproduced as printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 27, section 8.4.1 and Figure 12(a); p. 20, section 6.4.1, offline fluency-test definition.

outcomes.name: Average syntactic and semantic quality of questions generated during training
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same two researcher coders used for cue evaluation scored children’s questions; one was experienced with the grids and one was a novice (p. 17, section 6.1; p. 18, section 6.2). Each participant’s outcome is the average score across their training questions, with coder disagreements averaged. Section 6.2.3 states a 2-to-8-point scale and inter-rater reliability of 76.8% (p. 19); Appendix D gives the semantic and syntactic scoring rules (p. 32). Figure 10(b) instead labels the axis Average score per question (max=9) (p. 24, figure inspected directly). This internal scale discrepancy is unresolved. Coded as usefulness because the codebook includes output quality in that construct.

contrasts.reported: No significant difference between hand-crafted and GPT-3 incentive agents: t=0.57, p-value=0.57 and power=0.08. The t statistic is reproduced in the source’s comparison order.
contrasts.locator: p. 25, section 8.2.2; p. 24, Figure 10(b); p. 19, section 6.2.3; p. 32, Appendix D.

contrasts.reported: No significant difference between GPT-3 incentive and GPT-3 open agents: t=-0.81, p-value=0.41 and power=0.12. The t statistic is reproduced in the source’s comparison order.
contrasts.locator: p. 25, section 8.2.2; p. 24, Figure 10(b); p. 19, section 6.2.3; p. 32, Appendix D.

contrasts.reported: No significant difference between hand-crafted incentive and GPT-3 open agents: t=-0.29, p-value=0.77 and power=0.06. The t statistic is reproduced in the source’s comparison order.
contrasts.locator: p. 25, section 8.2.2; p. 24, Figure 10(b); p. 19, section 6.2.3; p. 32, Appendix D.

eligibility.reason: The child study uses an unspecified pseudo-randomized allocation method after baseline profiling, so actual random assignment is unconfirmed (p. 18, section 6.2.1). It explicitly reports 75 recruited children and assigned group sizes of 24, 26, and 25, but not final analyzed counts; the analyzed-person threshold therefore remains unclear and is not inferred from the reported degrees of freedom (p. 18, section 6.2.1; pp. 24-25, sections 8.2.1-8.2.2; p. 27, section 8.4.1). Divergent-question percentages, syntactic/semantic question quality, and offline divergent-question fluency are scored on children’s actual output, meeting criterion 3 (pp. 18-20, sections 6.2.2-6.2.3 and 6.4.1; results pp. 24-25 and 27). Core eligibility remains unclear. The ai_vs_human context classification applies only to the separate cue-output comparison (pp. 5, 17-18, 21-23), not to the child study with unresolved allocation.

one_line_finding: In a study that recruited 75 children (final analyzed counts not stated; p. 18, section 6.2.1), open GPT-3 cues elicited a higher percentage of divergent questions than hand-crafted incentive cues (t=-3.17, p-value=0.003; p. 24, section 8.2.1), with actual random assignment unconfirmed.
